summary:
Let `best[i]` be the highest score on landing on stone `i`. You arrive from one of the `k` stones before it, so
`best[i] = stones[i] + max(best[i−k..i−1])`. That max is a sliding-window maximum over the `best` values
already computed, so a monotonic deque gives it in O(1) amortised: O(n) overall.

question.md:
You start on stone 0, must end on the last stone, and each step jumps forward 1 to `k` stones. Your score is
the sum of the stones you land on, including the first and last. Return the maximum score.

- **Negative stones can't always be avoided**: if a run of more than `k − 1` negatives lies in the way, you
  must land on some of them.
- **One stone** means the score is just `stones[0]`.
- **Up to 10⁵ stones and `k` up to 10⁵**, so `n × k` can reach 10¹⁰. The score fits in 64 bits.

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- One stone: its value is the score.
- All negative stones: you still must land on the first and last; minimise the damage in between.
- `k ≥ n`: jump straight from the first stone to the last.

think.md:
**Dynamic programming.** Let `best[i]` be the highest score ending on stone `i`. You arrive at `i` from one of the
previous `k` stones, so `best[i] = stones[i] + max(best[i−k … i−1])`. Greedy choices (always jumping to the best
nearby stone) can fail; the DP considers every way to arrive.

**The bottleneck** is the maximum over the last `k` values, recomputed for every stone. That's a **sliding window
maximum** over the `best` array.

**The monotonic deque.** For a sliding window's maximum, an element that is **older and not larger** than a newer one
can never be the maximum again: the newer one is at least as large and stays in the window longer. So keep a deque of
indices whose values **decrease** from front to back:

- **back:** before adding an element, pop smaller-or-equal elements from the back (they're dominated);
- **front:** pop the front when it falls out of the window;
- the **front** is always the current window's maximum.

Each index enters and leaves the deque once: O(n) total. Storing indices (not values) is what lets us tell when the
front has left the window.

approaches.title: Dynamic programming, scanning back k stones

idea.md: Fill `best[i]` by scanning back over the previous `k` stones for the largest `best`.

build: For each stone, scan back up to `k` stones.
Add the stone's value to the best found.

lines.text: `best[0]`: you start on stone 0, so its value is always counted.
Stones in order: every take-off stone is computed before it's needed.
The best landing score among the stones you could have jumped from.
Land on stone `i` from that best take-off point.
The score on the last stone.

complexity.md: **Time O(n · k):** 10¹⁰ for the largest inputs. **Space O(n).**

steps.text: Stone 1: look back at best[0..0] = [2]; the top is 2 (stone 0). best[1] = -5 + 2 = -3.
Stone 2: look back at best[0..1] = [2, -3]; the top is 2 (stone 0). best[2] = -3 + 2 = -1.
Stone 3: look back at best[1..2] = [-3, -1]; the top is -1 (stone 2). best[3] = 4 + -1 = 3.
Stone 4: look back at best[2..3] = [-1, 3]; the top is 3 (stone 3). best[4] = -6 + 3 = -3.
Stone 5: look back at best[3..4] = [3, -3]; the top is 3 (stone 3). best[5] = -1 + 3 = 2.
Stone 6: look back at best[4..5] = [-3, 2]; the top is 2 (stone 5). best[6] = 3 + 2 = 5.

walk.title: best[i] = the top score on arriving at stone i = stones[i] + the best of the 2 stones before it. Check all k every time.

limits.md: The back-scan is a sliding window maximum recomputed from scratch each time.

approaches.title: Dynamic programming with a monotonic deque

idea.md:
Same DP, but keep a monotonic deque of indices with decreasing `best` values over the last `k` stones. The
front is the best predecessor; expire it when it's more than `k` back; after computing `best[i]`, pop
dominated entries from the back and push `i`.

build: Expire the front if too far.

lines.text: `best[0]` and a deque holding stone 0, the only take-off point so far.

notes.java: The deque is an array with `head`/`tail`; each index enters once.
notes.c: The deque is an array with `head`/`tail`; each index enters once.

lines.text: A stone more than `k` back can't be jumped from any more. Only one stone falls out of range per step, so one check suffices.
The front has the highest `best` among stones in range: take off from it.

Stones at the back with `best ≤ best[i]` are older (they'll go out of range sooner) and no better, so they'll never be the front again. Remove them, then add `i`. The deque is never empty when the front is read, since `i − 1` is always in range.
The highest score landing on the last stone.

complexity.md: **Time O(n).** **Space O(n)** for `best` (the deque holds at most `k`).

steps.text: Stone 1: The front (stone 0, best 2) is the best take-off: best[1] = -5 + 2 = -3.
Stone 2: The front (stone 0, best 2) is the best take-off: best[2] = -3 + 2 = -1. Stones [1] at the back are no better and older: drop them.
Stone 3: stone 0 is out of reach, drop it. The front (stone 2, best -1) is the best take-off: best[3] = 4 + -1 = 3. Stones [2] at the back are no better and older: drop them.
Stone 4: The front (stone 3, best 3) is the best take-off: best[4] = -6 + 3 = -3.
Stone 5: The front (stone 3, best 3) is the best take-off: best[5] = -1 + 3 = 2. Stones [4] at the back are no better and older: drop them.
Stone 6: stone 3 is out of reach, drop it. The front (stone 5, best 2) is the best take-off: best[6] = 3 + 2 = 5. Stones [5] at the back are no better and older: drop them.

walk.title: Same recurrence, but the 'best of the last k' is a sliding-window maximum: keep a deque of stones whose best values decrease front to back.

takeaways.md:
- **DP over a window of previous states:** speed up the max (or min) with a monotonic deque.
- "Jump 1 to k steps" means "take the best of the last k states".
- **Pitfall:** greedy jumps to the best nearby stone, which can lead into a worse stretch later.
